model.name: DREAM S2 semantic news-cycle retention
model.lambda_interpretation: lambda = elapsed hours since semantic topic attention peak
model.abstraction_layer: Raw RSS articles are converted into stable semantic topic objects before S2 fitting.
model.semantic_layer: Sparse TF-IDF article vectors, entity sets, keyword distributions, semantic connected components, centroid inertia, and a persistent topic_memory.json file.
model.event_horizon_layer: H(t)=Deviation(t)*CrossScaleCoherence(t), with Deviation=observed/expected_S2 and CrossScaleCoherence from source-tier spread, source diversity, and semantic coherence. Pre-horizon alerts require high H and positive slope.
model.signal_preprocessing: Formal S2 fit uses circadian-corrected publish-time article counts: raw count divided by expected global publishing/activity factor.
model.observation_clock: article.published_at, not GitHub Action run time
model.history_role: data/history.json retains raw article records and first_seen/last_seen provenance; topic_memory.json retains semantic identity; cycles.json retains completed S2 cycle summaries.
model.comparison: Delta AIC = AIC(exponential beta=1) - AIC(stretched S2 beta free)
model.cycle_archive_role: data/cycles.json stores deduplicated completed formal cycle summaries so prior S2 learning remains visible when a new wave resets the current topic. Current waves are not archived until replaced by a new peak.

articles.title: Trump ‘whiplash’ on deportations putting Afghans in turmoil: ‘People already survived a war’
articles.summary: Members of Congress and advocates warn that returning people to their home countries could be a death sentence Dozens of Afghans who are currently in the US but fear being deported back to Afghanistan along with a larger group and possibly killed by the Taliban are experiencing “fragile relief” this weekend after it appeared that the Trump administration had put on hold plans to remove them within days. Members of Congress and advocates have repeatedly warned that the deportations could effectively be a death sentence. Continue reading...

articles.title: Underwater salt mine closure in Ohio raises safety and supply concerns for winter
articles.summary: Questions remain about reason for leak, safety of drinking water and where salt can be sourced for roads during winter When water last month began gushing through a crack in the ceiling of a Morton Salt mine in Ohio, the company had only one option: shut the mine down for good. For locals in and around Fairport Harbor, it means the loss of 77 jobs; but for the wider region, which depends on its salt reserves to keep roads ice- and snow-free every winter, it could mean travel chaos. Continue reading...

articles.title: Choking fires, deadly heat and devastating floods: 2026 in extreme weather
articles.summary: People around the world have contended with unprecedented weather events and their fatal effects caused by the climate catastrophe After the world’s hottest summer since records began in 1850, the death toll from extreme weather in 2026 is already in the high tens of thousands. That is a conservative estimate and is certain to rise much higher. As Cop31 continues and scientists warn that climate breakdown may be accelerating , the Guardian looks back at a year of droughts, fires and floods as a reminder that, unless the world takes urgent action to cut emissions, this disastrous year will be one of the best of the rest of our lives. Continue reading...

articles.title: Interest rate rises likely in coming months, Bank of England’s chief economist says
articles.summary: ‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% last month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said. Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.
